title: Cabinet clears $ 5.12 m procurement of cardiac and diabetes medicines | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:27
-     - 0

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved the procurement of two essential medicines for cardiac and diabetic patients at a combined cost of around $ 5.12 million, following international competitive bidding.

The approvals cover 920,000 pre-filled syringes/vials of Enoxaparin Sodium Injection, used in the treatment of cardiac patients, and 2.7 million vials of Biphasic Isophane Insulin Injection for diabetic patients.

The Enoxaparin procurement has been awarded to China’s Shenzhen Techdow Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd., for $ 828,000, including Cost and Freight (C&F), after seven bids were received and evaluated. The company was identified as the substantially responsive lowest bidder.

The insulin procurement has been awarded to India’s M.J. Biopharm Ltd., for $ 4.293 million, including C&F, following the receipt of two bids. The company was the only substantially responsive bidder.

Both awards were approved on the recommendation of the High-Level Standing Procurement Committee, following evaluation of the bids, the Government said. 

The proposals to this effect were submitted by the Health Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa.

title: Sri Lanka–Nordic Business Council marks 25 years, elects new President | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:17
-     - 0

The Sri Lanka–Nordic Business Council marked its 25th Annual General Meeting, celebrating a quarter-century of strengthening business relations between Sri Lanka and the Nordic countries. Maleena Awn, Director of Operations at Meridian Maritime Services Ltd., was elected President for 2026/27.

The AGM was attended by Chief Guest Royal Norwegian Embassy in New Delhi Embassy Secretary, Political Affairs Tormod Nuland, and featured a keynote address by Norwegian Foreign Affairs Ministry Senior Adviser Aneela Shah Khan. Honorary Consul General of Norway Mano Sekeram was also present.

In her address, Shah Khan noted that Sri Lankan exports to Norway reached nearly $ 62 million in 2025, registering a 20% increase over 2024. She pointed to opportunities for greater cooperation in areas such as maritime services, renewable energy and technology, citing the collaboration between Colombo Dockyard and Norway’s Misje Eco Bulk on hybrid vessels as an example of the potential for partnerships between the two countries. 

She also highlighted Norway’s support for Sri Lanka in areas including entrepreneurship, skills development and sustainable business practices, stressing the importance of policy predictability and transparency in attracting investment.

Outgoing President Shaameel Mohideen reflected on the Council’s work over the past 25 years, noting the importance of its role in connecting businesses and creating opportunities for engagement with the Nordic region. He highlighted the region’s strengths in innovation, renewable energy, digitalisation and sustainable development as areas with scope for greater collaboration.

Setting out her priorities for the year ahead, incoming President Awn said the Council would place greater emphasis on translating business connections into commercial partnerships. Plans include targeted trade delegations, stronger links with Nordic chambers and trade promotion organisations, and greater support for SMEs seeking access to Nordic markets. 

She also identified opportunities for knowledge exchange and business collaboration in digitalisation, clean technology, automation, tourism, renewable energy, maritime services and logistics.

The new office bearers for 2026/27 include; Senior Vice President Priyantha Subasinghe (Kalaro- Managing Director), Vice President Chrishan De Mel (99X- Chief Marketing and Corporate Affairs Officer), and Treasurer Dr. D.S.K. Pathirana (Sri Lanka National Technology Development Cooperative- Chairman). Shaameel Mohideen (Spillburg Holdings- Director) will serve as Immediate Past President.

The Council’s committee includes representatives from Dart Global Logistics, LGL Marketing Services, Lion Brewery, Maliban Healthcare and Scan Global Logistics, with Physio Medicare and Propylon One serving by invitation. Prasath Mahalingam and Bobby Jordan Hansen continue as Honorary Members.

title: CAA tells Parliament panel it has no power to set domestic gas prices | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:16
-     - 4

The Consumer Affairs Authority (CAA) has told a parliamentary committee that it has no power to determine domestic gas prices, after a private distributor significantly raised the price of its domestic gas cylinder, the Parliament Secretariat said.

Officials of the Ministry of Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Cooperative Development and the CAA were summoned before the Sectoral Oversight Committee on Environment, Agriculture and Resource Sustainability on Wednesday to discuss the increase. The meeting was chaired by Committee Chair MP Hector Appuhamy.

The CAA Chairman said the Authority had stepped in because of the difficulties the increase caused consumers, although it lacked the power to set prices. He said the company had agreed to reduce the price after discussions with the Authority.

According to the CAA Chairman, the company said that because its share of the domestic gas market was relatively small, it had to buy gas at a higher price and had raised its cylinder prices in line with the higher purchase cost.

The Committee urged the CAA to ensure that decisions on domestic gas prices do not cause difficulties for consumers. It also stressed the need to ensure an uninterrupted supply of domestic gas in the future and to take the necessary steps to protect consumers from price increases, the Parliament Secretariat said.

MPs Upul Kithsiri, M.A.C.S. Chathuri Gangani, Susantha Kumara Navaratne, Sudath Balagalla, Kitnan Selvaraj and Gnanamuththu Srineshan also attended the meeting.

title: Sri Lanka’s Budget 2027: From economic recovery to better livelihoods | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 03:47
-     - 12

Ultimately, the success of Budget 2027 should be measured not merely by how much revenue the Government collects, but by how effectively that revenue improves the lives of the people of Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka's future lies not merely in tax revenue, but in production, investment, employment, entrepreneurship, fiscal discipline and public confidence. Budget 2027 must therefore become an opportunity to transform economic recovery into genuine and lasting prosperity for the nation

Sri Lanka’s Budget 2027 represents an important attempt to move the country beyond economic stabilisation towards a more sustainable model of economic transformation. Following years of financial crisis, fiscal adjustment and considerable hardship among households and businesses, the central challenge is no longer simply restoring macroeconomic stability. It is translating that stability into higher productivity, stronger investment, employment opportunities and improved living standards. 

Presented under the theme “A Thriving Nation – A Beautiful Life”, Budget 2027 seeks to strengthen economic growth while addressing the expectations of citizens who continue to experience the consequences of the economic crisis. Its success, however, will ultimately depend not on the scale of financial allocations announced, but on the effectiveness with which these resources are converted into measurable economic and social outcomes.

Fiscal consolidation and the challenge of sustainable growth

The Government has estimated revenue and grants of Rs. 6,180 billion for 2027, against total expenditure of Rs. 7,933 billion. The resulting budget deficit is Rs. 1,753 billion, equivalent to approximately 4.5% of GDP. The expenditure figure includes additional provisions associated with the reconstruction requirements arising from Cyclone Ditwah. The underlying expenditure estimate is Rs. 7,673 billion, with a further Rs. 260 billion carried forward through supplementary provisions. Public investment has been allocated Rs. 2,000 billion, including provisions associated with reconstruction. 

This represents a significant commitment to capital expenditure at a time when the country continues to face considerable fiscal constraints. The Government has established a medium-term objective of achieving economic growth of 7% or higher, maintaining revenue at not less than 16% of GDP and gradually increasing it towards 20% in the longer term. These objectives are important, but their achievement requires a careful balance between revenue mobilisation, expenditure management, debt sustainability and economic expansion. 

Government revenue is estimated at approximately 15.8% of GDP in 2027. Although this represents a substantial improvement from the levels experienced during the crisis, achieving the medium-term revenue target remains challenging. 

At the same time, interest payments continue to absorb a significant portion of public resources. The estimated allocation for interest payments is Rs. 2,643 billion, highlighting the continuing burden of public debt on fiscal space. The policy challenge is therefore twofold: increasing revenue without unnecessarily burdening productive economic activity, and improving expenditure efficiency so that public resources generate greater economic and social returns.

Moving beyond tax revenue towards a production-based economy

Tax revenue remains essential for maintaining fiscal stability, financing public services and reducing dependence on borrowing. Nevertheless, a sustainable increase in revenue cannot rely exclusively on higher tax rates or additional taxation of existing compliant taxpayers. Sri Lanka requires a broader and more productive economic base capable of generating employment, exports, investment and taxable income. 

The proposed personal income tax revisions represent an important step towards providing relief to individual taxpayers. From 1 April 2027, the annual tax-free threshold is proposed to increase from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 1.95 million, equivalent to a monthly threshold of Rs. 162,500. The revised progressive tax structure introduces a 12% tax band and widens several existing income brackets. The maximum marginal tax rate remains 36%, but the income level at which it applies is increased. These changes provide additional relief to salaried employees and other individual taxpayers, particularly those in the middle-income categories. They may also help improve disposable income and ease some household financial pressures. 

However, the long-term sustainability of personal income tax relief depends on broadening the tax base, improving compliance and bringing more economic activity into the formal system. The Government must therefore strengthen digital tax administration, improve information-sharing between institutions and reduce opportunities for tax evasion, while ensuring that compliant taxpayers are treated fairly.MA more transparent, predictable and efficient tax system would strengthen taxpayer confidence and improve the environment for private investment.

Investment incentives and export competitiveness

Private sector investment is essential for Sri Lanka to achieve sustained economic growth. Public investment alone cannot generate the scale of employment, innovation and export expansion required for economic transformation. Budget 2027 proposes enhanced capital allowances for eligible Board of Investment-approved enterprises engaged in export-oriented manufacturing and tourism development activities. 

Qualifying enterprises with a minimum investment of $ 3 million may opt for an enhanced capital allowance equivalent to 200% of qualifying capital expenditure, subject to the prescribed conditions. This proposal could strengthen the attractiveness of Sri Lanka as an investment destination, particularly for export-oriented manufacturing, tourism infrastructure and other productive activities. 

Nevertheless, tax incentives are only one component of the investment decision. Investors also require policy consistency, efficient administrative procedures, reliable energy supply, competitive logistics, skilled labour, access to finance and a predictable regulatory environment. Investment incentives should therefore be evaluated against measurable outcomes such as additional capital formation, export earnings, employment creation, technology transfer and productivity improvements. 

A well-designed incentive framework should reward genuinely additional investment rather than provide concessions for activities that would have taken place without them.

Youth, entrepreneurship and the capital market

One of the notable proposals in Budget 2027 is the “A Share for Everyone” initiative, which seeks to introduce eligible students aged 18 and above to investment in the Colombo Stock Exchange through a share allocation valued at Rs. 10,000. This initiative has the potential to promote financial literacy, investment awareness and long-term savings among young people. 

However, its value should extend beyond the distribution of shares. Students should also be provided with appropriate education on capital markets, investment risks, financial planning, corporate governance and responsible investment. The proposed SME Listing Support Mechanism is another important initiative. It could encourage smaller enterprises to access capital markets, improve corporate governance and reduce excessive dependence on conventional bank financing. 

For Sri Lanka, developing a broader investment culture and strengthening capital market participation are important elements of financial inclusion and economic modernisation.

MSMEs: Financing the engines of employment

Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) remain among the most important contributors to employment, regional economic activity and household income. Budget 2027 allocates approximately Rs. 67.7 billion for interest subsidies and refinancing arrangements intended to facilitate around Rs. 174 billion in concessionary financing for MSMEs through State and private banking institutions. These financing arrangements are expected to support working capital requirements, investment in machinery, technology improvements, business expansion and employment creation. 

The effectiveness of these programs, however, depends on more than the availability of funds. Entrepreneurs must be able to access financing through transparent, simplified and practical procedures. Credit assessment should recognise the realities of small businesses while maintaining appropriate safeguards against excessive lending and non-performing loans. 

Financial assistance should also be complemented by business development services, accounting and financial management support, digitalisation, market access and export readiness. Particular attention should be given to women-led enterprises, rural businesses, young entrepreneurs and enterprises operating in sectors with significant employment potential. The objective should be to transform MSMEs from survival-oriented businesses into productive, competitive and sustainable enterprises.

Infrastructure, housing and regional development

Infrastructure investment is an essential foundation for economic transformation. Budget 2027 allocates significant resources for roads, railways, rural connectivity, water supply, housing and regional development. The allocation of Rs. 251 billion for highways and railway development reflects the importance attached to transport infrastructure and connectivity. Improved transport networks can reduce logistics costs, facilitate movement of goods, connect producers with markets and strengthen tourism and regional economic activity. 

However, infrastructure investment should not be evaluated merely by the number of projects commenced or completed. Its economic value depends on whether it reduces production costs, improves access to markets and generates sustainable benefits. Housing is another important component of the Budget. 

Under the “A Place of One’s Own – A Beautiful Life” program, the Government aims to construct 70,000 houses for low-income households, including 10,000 houses during 2027. The assistance per house is proposed to increase from Rs. 1 million to Rs. 1.5 million. Housing programs can improve living standards, create employment in construction and related industries, and support local economic activity. 

Nevertheless, implementation should be supported by transparent beneficiary selection, appropriate infrastructure, access to essential services and effective monitoring of construction quality. Regional development must also receive sustained attention. 

Economic growth cannot be concentrated exclusively in Colombo and other major urban centres. The allocation of Rs. 50 billion for district development programs provides an opportunity to strengthen regional infrastructure, improve local economic activity and address disparities in development.

Health, education and human capital

Economic growth is closely linked to the quality of human capital. Budget 2027 allocates Rs. 131 billion for capital expenditure in the health sector, while education-related allocations include Rs. 35 billion. These investments should be viewed not merely as public expenditure but as long-term investments in productivity, workforce quality and national development. A healthy population, a skilled workforce and a quality education system are essential for attracting investment and sustaining economic competitiveness. 

Sri Lanka must also address the growing importance of technical education, digital skills, vocational training and industry-oriented qualifications. The education system should increasingly connect learning with employment opportunities, entrepreneurship and the skills required by emerging industries. Improving public health services, educational access and the quality of human resources would strengthen the country's ability to participate in higher-value economic activities.

Agriculture, fisheries and the rural economy

Agriculture and fisheries remain important sources of livelihood, particularly in rural and coastal communities. Budget 2027 allocates Rs. 6.2 billion for fisheries sector development, including fishery harbour infrastructure, research and inland fisheries development. 

The Government has also set an objective of increasing fisheries export earnings from $ 300 million to $ 600 million by 2030. Achieving this target requires more than financial allocations. The sector needs modern technology, improved cold-chain facilities, quality assurance, export certification, sustainable resource management and stronger market access. Similarly, agricultural development should increasingly focus on productivity, value addition, technology adoption, storage facilities, efficient distribution and reducing post-harvest losses. 

The objective must be to move beyond subsistence-oriented production towards commercially viable, competitive and market-oriented agriculture. Rural economic development should therefore be integrated with transport infrastructure, financial services, digital connectivity and entrepreneurship.

Digitalisation, tax administration and public accountability

Digital transformation is becoming an essential component of economic competitiveness and public sector efficiency. Budget 2027 increases the allocation for the digital economy to Rs. 28.5 billion, supporting institutional strengthening, digital Government transformation, digital industry development and wider adoption of digital services. 

The expansion of digital public services could reduce administrative costs, improve transparency and make Government services more accessible to citizens and businesses. Digitalisation also has significant implications for tax administration.An integrated digital tax system, supported by reliable taxpayer information, electronic transactions, improved data analytics and effective compliance monitoring, can help broaden the tax base and reduce revenue leakage. 

However, digital transformation must be accompanied by institutional reform, data protection, cybersecurity, staff capacity development and appropriate governance arrangements. Public accountability is equally important. Every major Budget program should have clearly defined implementation deadlines, responsible institutions, measurable performance indicators and transparent monitoring arrangements. 

The public should be able to assess not only how much money has been allocated, but also what has been achieved through those allocations. Regular reporting on project progress, expenditure performance, employment outcomes and economic benefits would strengthen public confidence and improve fiscal accountability.

From Budget allocations to measurable economic outcomes

Budget 2027 provides opportunities to strengthen economic recovery through investment, entrepreneurship, infrastructure development, social protection and digital transformation. 

However, the ultimate success of the Budget cannot be measured solely by the volume of revenue collected or expenditure incurred. The more important questions are whether businesses become more productive, whether new employment opportunities are created, whether household incomes improve, whether exports expand and whether the cost-of-living pressures faced by citizens are meaningfully reduced. 

Sri Lanka must also ensure that economic growth is inclusive. Vulnerable households, low-income earners, persons with disabilities, elderly citizens and communities affected by economic or natural disasters require effective and targeted support. Social protection programs should be designed to protect those who genuinely need assistance while strengthening opportunities for economic participation and self-reliance. At the same time, fiscal discipline, efficient public expenditure and responsible debt management must remain central to the country's economic policy.

Conclusion: From revenue mobilisation to real economic prosperity

Sri Lanka's economic recovery has created an opportunity to move towards a more productive, investment-oriented and inclusive economy. Budget 2027 seeks to support this transition through personal income tax relief, MSME financing, investment incentives, housing, infrastructure, health, education, agriculture, fisheries and digitalisation. The challenge now is implementation. Government institutions must translate Budget proposals into practical programs, while the private sector must respond through investment, innovation, entrepreneurship and employment creation. 

Financial institutions, professional bodies and other stakeholders also have an important role in supporting productive investment, strengthening financial management and improving business competitiveness. The country's future cannot depend exclusively on increasing tax revenue or expanding public expenditure. Sustainable prosperity must be built through production, investment, productivity, employment, entrepreneurship, fiscal discipline and public confidence. 

Ultimately, the success of Budget 2027 should be measured not merely by how much revenue the Government collects, but by how effectively that revenue improves the lives of the people of Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka's future lies not merely in tax revenue, but in production, investment, employment, entrepreneurship, fiscal discipline and public confidence. Budget 2027 must therefore become an opportunity to transform economic recovery into genuine and lasting prosperity for the nation.

(The author is Managing Partner of A.G. Sarma, Chartered Accountants)

title: Stop financial bleeding before expanding SriLankan Airlines | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 03:39
-     - 15

SriLankan Airlines has once again announced an ambitious five-year plan aimed at restoring profitability, expanding its fleet and improving operational efficiency.

The plan was discussed before Parliament’s Sectoral Oversight Committee on Infrastructure and Strategic Development, where attention was given to aircraft shortages, technical delays, mounting debt and procurement difficulties.

These are undoubtedly serious matters requiring immediate attention. However, there is another equally important question that deserves national discussion.

Before expanding the airline, have we properly identified and stopped the financial leakages, unnecessary expenditure, poor management practices and potential irregularities that may be contributing to its continuing losses?

A simple business principle that should not be ignored

Imagine running a small shop that continuously loses money. Would the first solution be to open another five branches, purchase additional equipment and employ more staff? Certainly not.

Any responsible business owner would first examine the accounts, identify where money is being lost, investigate unnecessary expenses and take immediate corrective action.

Only after bringing the existing business under control would expansion become a sensible option. Why should this basic principle be any different for SriLankan Airlines?

An airline is undoubtedly more complex than a small shop. Aircraft availability, network connectivity and operational reliability are essential to generating revenue. Nevertheless, expanding a business that is already making substantial losses without properly addressing its underlying weaknesses could increase the financial burden rather than resolve it.

Billions lost, yet fundamental questions remain

According to the Finance Ministry’s Mid-Year Fiscal Position Report, SriLankan Airlines recorded a loss before tax of approximately Rs. 35.6 billion during the first three months of the 2026/27 financial year.

The same report identified substantial increases in fuel expenditure, foreign exchange losses and continuing structural financial difficulties.

Meanwhile, the President has reportedly informed Parliament that the airline’s accumulated losses between 2008 and 2025 reached approximately Rs. 528 billion. These figures should concern every Sri Lankan citizen.

The airline’s financial problems cannot simply be attributed to corruption or management failures. Fuel prices, exchange rates, aircraft maintenance, financing costs and international disruptions all have significant consequences.

However, these external challenges should not prevent a thorough investigation into expenditure that management can actually control. Why are overseas stations and GSA contracts not receiving greater attention?

One area that deserves particular scrutiny is SriLankan Airlines’ overseas station operations, including General Sales Agent (GSA) agreements, ground handling arrangements, staffing structures and other contracted services.

Across international stations, expenditure is often incurred in foreign currencies such as Singapore dollars, US dollars and euros.

When converted into Sri Lankan rupees, even relatively small amounts of avoidable expenditure can become substantial.

Are all overseas GSA arrangements still commercially necessary? Are the services being billed actually delivered? Are staffing levels justified by the workload? Are contracts being regularly reviewed against market rates? Could some activities be managed more efficiently through alternative arrangements?

These are not accusations against every GSA or overseas station. Many such arrangements are essential and provide valuable services.

However, every agreement involving the airline’s money should be independently examined to establish whether it represents genuine value.

Where there are credible allegations of overbilling, unsupported invoices, conflicts of interest or services not delivered, they should be investigated using contracts, invoices, duty rosters, operational reports and payment records.

Any wrongdoing established through proper investigation must lead to accountability and, where legally possible, the recovery of funds.

An independent audit must come before major expansion decisions

The airline should commission a genuinely independent financial and operational audit, prioritising areas of greatest risk across its major departments and overseas operations.

This examination should include aircraft leasing, maintenance expenditure, procurement, crew accommodation, transportation, station administration, staffing, GSA contracts and ground handling agreements.

The objective must not simply be to produce another report that remains on a shelf.

The findings should identify unnecessary expenditure, weaknesses in internal controls, commercially unjustified contracts and opportunities for immediate savings.

The Government should also establish a clear process for referring suspected criminal conduct to the appropriate independent authorities.

An investigation must be based on evidence, conducted transparently and remain free from political interference.

Fleet expansion alone cannot guarantee profitability

The proposal to increase the fleet from 23 aircraft to at least 29 by 2029 may be operationally justified.

Aircraft shortages can cause delays, cancellations, missed connections, additional accommodation expenses and serious damage to customer confidence.

However, additional aircraft also introduce leasing costs, maintenance commitments, insurance, staffing requirements and other financial obligations.

Therefore, every aircraft acquisition should be supported by a transparent business case demonstrating expected revenue, route profitability, operating costs and financial risks.

The airline must also review routes that consistently perform poorly, aircraft utilisation, scheduling efficiency, maintenance planning, cargo opportunities and revenue management.

A larger fleet is not necessarily a healthier airline.

The objective should be a financially sustainable airline, not simply a bigger airline.

Accountability must begin at management level

SriLankan Airlines has experienced numerous leadership changes and restructuring proposals over the years.

Each new leadership team arrives with expectations of improvement, yet the underlying financial difficulties remain.

The time has come to move beyond announcements and establish measurable accountability.

Every department should have clearly defined financial and operational targets.

Senior management should be required to explain significant budget overruns, recurring inefficiencies and failures to implement agreed corrective measures.

A confidential and independently supervised reporting mechanism should also protect employees and former employees who provide credible evidence of financial irregularities or misconduct.

Those raising legitimate concerns should not face retaliation merely for requesting an investigation.

A practical roadmap to recovery

A credible recovery plan should begin with immediate action rather than waiting several years for results.

Within the first 90 days, the Government should initiate independent reviews of expenditure presenting significant financial risks, major overseas contracts and areas where credible financial irregularities have been reported.

Within six months, the airline should begin implementing verified cost-saving measures, renegotiating unjustified expenditure and correcting weaknesses in procurement and financial controls.

Within 12 months, management should publish measurable results showing savings achieved, operational improvements, route performance and progress towards financial sustainability.

The longer-term fleet and network strategy should proceed alongside these measures, but every major investment must be justified by independently reviewed financial projections.

Parliament should receive regular progress reports, with sufficient information made public to demonstrate that genuine corrective action is taking place.

The people of Sri Lanka deserve better

Sri Lanka is a country where many families continue to struggle with the cost of living.

Public resources are precious, and every rupee committed to supporting a State enterprise that continues to make losses carries an opportunity cost.

That money could otherwise support healthcare, education, infrastructure and essential public services.

SriLankan Airlines remains an important national institution, with experienced employees, international connections and the potential to contribute meaningfully to tourism and the economy.

Its dedicated workforce should not be unfairly blamed for failures beyond its control.

But protecting the airline must also mean protecting public money.

The Government, Parliament, Finance Ministry and airline leadership have a responsibility to ensure that recovery is built on transparency, financial discipline, operational efficiency and accountability.

The question Parliament must answer

The five-year plan may contain worthwhile proposals. But the public deserves to know whether it includes a sufficiently independent investigation into existing expenditure, contracts and financial controls.

Before approving further major expansion, Parliament should demand clear answers.

Why is the airline losing money? Which losses are unavoidable, and which can be prevented? What has management already done to stop unnecessary expenditure? Who is responsible for implementing corrective action, and how will success be measured?

SriLankan Airlines does not need another recovery plan that merely promises a brighter future.

It needs a recovery program that identifies the real problems, takes corrective action and demonstrates measurable results.

Stop the financial bleeding. Investigate the leakages. Eliminate unnecessary expenditure. Establish accountability. Restore financial discipline. Then expand responsibly.

That is how SriLankan Airlines can begin rebuilding its financial strength, public confidence and long-term future.

(The author is a former SriLankan Airlines Representative in Singapore, with over 13 years of aviation experience at Changi Airport)

title: Seizing new opportunities in China’s development, writing a new chapter in China-Sri Lanka cooperation | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 03:14
-     - 15

Guided by the principles of mutual respect, fairness and justice, we will work together to overcome obstacles and rise to the challenges, implement the common understandings reached by the two countries’ leaders in a practical manner, walk side by side on the path to modernisation, and continue to advance our strategic cooperative partnership featuring sincere mutual assistance and everlasting friendship. Together, we will work towards building a China-Sri Lanka community with a shared future

The year 2026 marks the launch of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan for economic and social development. Against the backdrop of a sluggish global economic recovery and ongoing international turbulence, China’s economy has pressed ahead under pressure, maintaining overall stability while making steady progress and breaking new ground amid global changes, showcasing a promising outlook. China’s recently released economic report for the first three quarters of the year once again delivered a stronger-than-expected performance, demonstrating the resilience and high quality of its growth. This is further proof that China’s economy enjoys bright prospects, robust growth momentum and a promising future.

Snapshot of China’s key achievements in recent times

First, the foundation for economic stability has continued to strengthen. In the first three quarters of 2026, China’s gross domestic product (GDP) reached 107.1 trillion yuan, up 4.6% year on year. The economy expanded by 5.7 trillion yuan, the largest increase in five years. This growth rate remains in a leading position among major global economies. Employment and prices remained generally stable, while people’s livelihoods continued to improve. China’s sound economic fundamentals and positive long-term growth trajectory has become even more evident.

Second, new growth drivers are gaining momentum. Emerging growth drivers, represented by high-end manufacturing, the digital economy and modern services, contributed more than 40% of China’s economic growth in the first three quarters of this year. China’s artificial intelligence (AI) sector has seen explosive growth. Open-source AI models developed in China have recorded more than 10 billion downloads worldwide. China accounts for over 90% of global humanoid robot shipments, while AI-related industries, including smart in-vehicle equipment, have maintained growth rates of over 30%. Embodied AI is also moving towards large-scale commercial applications. Multiple types of commercial rockets have been successfully launched, and technologies such as quantum information, integrated circuits, and nuclear fusion have been advancing at an accelerated pace. China is also stepping up its green transition. Energy consumption per unit of GDP fell by 3.1% year on year in the first three quarters. The retail penetration rate of new energy vehicles (NEVs) has remained above 60% for six consecutive months, with total sales exceeding 7.7 million units. Today, three out of every five new energy passenger vehicles sold worldwide are made in China.

Third, the benefits of deeper integration with the world economy are continuing to unfold. China remains committed to “sharing benefits with the whole world”. Through opening up at a higher level, China is embracing the broader trend of global development, injecting valuable vitality into the world economy and working with the international community to achieve shared development and prosperity. In the first three quarters of 2026, China’s total imports and exports of goods reached 39.94 trillion yuan, up 18.8% year on year, bucking the trend of sluggish global trade. Imports grew by 22.3%, significantly faster than exports, which rose by 16.4%. Trade with Belt and Road partner countries increased by 17.1%. China continues to expand institutional opening-up, extending zero-tariff treatment to 63 countries and promoting trade liberalisation and investment facilitation. The “Big Market for All: Export to China” initiative has created new channels for quality foreign goods and services to enter the Chinese market. Meanwhile, high-tech products made in China continue to support global industrial upgrading and the green transition, while making everyday life more convenient for people around the world.

President Anura Kumara Disanayake (left) with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, January 2025

China-Sri Lanka shared history of economic and trade cooperation 

These achievements clearly underscore that China remains a driving force of global economic growth and a stabiliser for the world economy, and more importantly a major engine for the development and revitalisation of the Global South. Both China and Sri Lanka are members of the Global South. The two countries have a long history of economic and trade cooperation and have achieved fruitful results, setting an example for South-South cooperation. Even before the establishment of diplomatic ties, China and Sri Lanka overcame numerous obstacles to sign the Rubber-Rice Pact, forging the spirit of “independence, self-reliance, solidarity and mutual assistance” enshrined in the Pact and laying a solid foundation for mutually-beneficial cooperation. Over nearly 70 years of diplomatic relations, the two countries have stood together through thick and thin and supported each other in times of need, while staying true to the spirit of the Rubber-Rice Pact. They have continued to deepen practical cooperation across various fields and worked together to advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, achieving fruitful results that promote national development, serve long-term interests and improve people's livelihoods.

Infrastructure connectivity has opened up new pathways for development. Port City Colombo, as Sri Lanka’s largest foreign direct investment (FDI) project to date, has attracted more than US$2 billion in investment and registered over 200 companies. The Colombo International Container Terminal (CICT) has become one of South Asia’s leading deep-water container terminals, handling a major share of the Port of Colombo’s total throughput. Hambantota International Port (HIP) has emerged as a world-class hub for vehicle roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) operations, with its annual container handling capacity set to reach 2 million TEUs in early 2027, further strengthening Sri Lanka’s ambition to become a regional maritime hub. The Lakvijaya Power Plant in Norochcholai, Puttalam, supplies a quarter of the country’s base-load electricity, bringing light to millions of households. The Northern road network, the Southern Expressway, the Southern Railway Line and the Central Expressway under construction are steadily expanding the transport links that underpin regional economic development. The completion of the Elahera water transfer tunnel has opened up a key section of Sri Lanka’s North Central Province Canal Project. Once the entire project is completed, it is expected to provide a reliable supply of irrigation and drinking water to 74,000 hectares of farmland and 375,000 households along its route, bringing new hope for development to the drought-prone northern regions.

People-centred assistance has improved livelihoods across the whole island. Since the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Sri Lanka, China has provided around 140 assistance projects and more than 60 batches of supplies to support people’s livelihoods in Sri Lanka. These have covered a wide range of areas, including housing, education, transport, healthcare, water supply and emergency disaster relief. Landmark buildings such as the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH), the Nelum Pokuna Mahinda Rajapaksa Theatre and the Supreme Court Complex have become enduring symbols of China-Sri Lanka friendship. The Outpatient Department Building of the National Hospital of Sri Lanka and the National Nephrology Specialised Hospital have both been put into operation, helping improve public health and well-being. A total of 1,996 subsidised housing units for low-income families are under construction, which will fulfil the dream of a secure home for those in need. The China-Sri Lanka Joint Research and Demonstration Centre for Water Technology (JRDC) is helping more local communities gain access to safe drinking water. China has also donated school uniform fabric for four consecutive years, benefiting more than 4.4 million students across the island. The Digital Transformation Project of General Education in Sri Lanka will establish 900 smart classrooms in 500 schools nationwide, helping bridge the digital divide in education. China’s MAZU intelligent meteorological early-warning system has also been deployed in Sri Lanka, providing technical support for tackling climate change and improving disaster prevention and mitigation. Emergency reconstruction of 14 bridges has also been launched, living up to people’s expectations on road connectivity in disaster-affected areas. 

Joint talent development has practiced the sharing of “fish” and “fishing”. China is dedicated to not only “giving others fish”, but also “teaching others to fish”. In addition to immediate assistance, China has also been supporting Sri Lanka in long-term capacity building and personnel training. Since 1983, China has provided training opportunities in China for nearly 14,000 Sri Lankan officials and business representatives. 

Over the past six years, the China Aid Training Program has enrolled an average of 1,000 Sri Lankan participants each year. The China-Sri Lanka South-South Cooperation Technical Assistance Project has been particularly successful. Since its launch three years ago, it has trained more than 2,000 Sri Lankan farmers and agricultural workers, boosting both the yields and incomes of banana, pineapple and mango cultivation. The 6 agricultural training videos produced under the project have also been incorporated into Sri Lanka’s national training curriculum, providing long-term support for the wider adoption of improved agricultural techniques.

Stand with China is to stand with opportunity

History and facts have proven, and will continue to prove that to stand with China is to stand with opportunity; to believe in China is to believe in tomorrow; and to invest in China is to invest in the future. China and Sri Lanka are fellow travelers on the path toward development and revitalisation, and good partners of win-win cooperation. China’s vibrant economic growth will definitely open up broader prospects for China-Sri Lanka practical cooperation and deliver greater benefits to our two peoples. China-Sri Lanka cooperation is built on the principle of mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit, and has made a significant contribution to promoting socioeconomic development and the people’s well-being of both sides. China has consistently provided support for Sri Lanka’s development in a spirit of sincerity and goodwill, with no political conditions imposed on any cooperation or assistance project. China is ready to work with Sri Lanka to foster a favourable business environment, encourage closer cooperation between enterprises of the two countries, and accelerate negotiations on a China-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement (FTA), upgrade China-Sri Lanka high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and jointly open up new space for win-win development of higher standard, stronger resilience and greater sustainability.

2027 milestone year

2027 will witness the 70th anniversary of China-Sri Lanka diplomatic relations and the 75th anniversary of the Rubber-Rice Pact, bringing a new milestone in China-Sri Lanka relations to build on past achievements and pave the way forward. The spirit of the Rubber-Rice Pact is a precious historical treasure of both sides in removing external irritants and lending sincere mutual support. In today’s changing world, it is more important than ever to carry forward and uphold this great spirit. China stands ready to work with Sri Lanka to draw wisdom from the history of our bilateral relations and strength from the spirit of the Rubber-Rice Pact. Guided by the principles of mutual respect, fairness and justice, we will work together to overcome obstacles and rise to the challenges, implement the common understandings reached by the two countries’ leaders in a practical manner, walk side by side on the path to modernisation, and continue to advance our strategic cooperative partnership featuring sincere mutual assistance and everlasting friendship. Together, we will work towards building a China-Sri Lanka community with a shared future.

title: Making aspiration affordable again: Notes from alternative Budget | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 02:59
-     - 15

As you read this, Sri Lankans are living through a historic redistribution of wealth. Evidence shows that since 2019 Sri Lanka has witnessed a redistribution of income away from the bottom and towards the top. An Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) analysis of Department of Census and Statistics data found that between 2019 and early 2025, the real household income of the poorest 20% fell by 19.6%, while that of the richest 20% increased by 6.8%. The difference is visible across the income distribution. Real median household income fell by 11.1%, compared with a decline of only 1.7% in the average household income.

As a consequence, the distance between the top and bottom widened sharply: in 2019, the average household in the richest 20% earned around 11.2 times as much as the average household in the poorest 20%; by early 2025, that ratio had risen to 14.8 times. Budget 2027 seems likely to accelerate this upward redistribution of wealth, there is little relief for working people, other than raising the income tax-free threshold from 150,000 to 162,500. Sri Lanka’s long-suffering middle class received little or no attention. 

An SJB alternative Budget should demonstrate what would change under its administration, restoring purchasing power to working and middle-income households would be a central objective. The SJB and Sajith Premadasa more specifically, has criticised the current program’s over-emphasis on fiscal consolidation, its failure to distinguish GDP growth from external-sector resilience, and the trajectory towards rebuilding a significant International Sovereign Bond (ISB) portfolio.

The Middle Class is the aspirational class: the salaried executive that wants to move closer to the city, into a home big enough to care for their parents in; the veteran electrician that saved up for decades to start his own business; parents saving up for a downpayment on a mortgage so they can finally own their own home, the high-earning senior manager with a 20-year career that dreams of buying a European sedan, a small-business owner trying to expand, a young couple that want to get married and start a family, but cannot afford to move our of their parent’s homes.

The data is clear: the Sri Lankan middle class is significantly diminished since the 2019 economic crisis saw 70% inflation and interest rates as high as 32% alongside a rapidly depreciating currency. Today, a salaried executive will struggle to afford rent in an urban enclave close to the main city, many skilled workers have already moved abroad, SMEs struggle under a pile of debt that has kept accumulating under moratoriums that came and went. Dynamic entrepreneurs have largely retreated into what’s left of the corporate sector. Beyond the economic indictors of stability lies the real cost of the economic crisis: the loss of aspiration, the surrendering of dreams.

Affordable family vehicle category

A basic family car should not be treated fiscally in the same way as a Land Cruiser or Mercedes Benz. Sri Lanka already differentiates vehicle excise according to engine capacity. A 1,301-1,500cc petrol hybrid currently attracts Rs. 3,450 per cc, compared with Rs. 9,650 per cc for a 2,751-3,000cc hybrid. Vehicles also face customs duty, customs surcharge, VAT and, where applicable, luxury tax. The alternative Budget would create a tightly defined Affordable Family Vehicle category:

This is a deliberately narrow category, aimed primarily at the lower-middle and middle-income family-car market rather than providing a concession across the entire vehicle market. Examples of vehicles in the Sri Lankan small-car market likely to fall within the category, subject to individual CIF values, include:

This also corresponds reasonably closely with current demand. In August 2026, around 96% of new car registrations were in the below 1,000cc/100kW small-car category. In September, 770 Wagon Rs were registered, while BYD registered 316 ATTO 1s. Phasing in the tax reduction over three years is necessary to maintain vehicle price stability. The concession would be implemented through scheduled reductions in excise and import taxation rather than an immediate removal of taxes. The objective should be a material reduction in the landed and retail price of qualifying vehicles over three years.

Prices would be reduced gradually over three years by lowering excise duties and customs duty and removing the 50% customs duty surcharge on qualifying affordable family vehicles. VAT and SSCL would remain unchanged, preserving a significant tax contribution while reducing the exceptionally high upfront cost of basic vehicle ownership.

Vehicle taxes remain a major revenue source, generating Rs. 387 billion in the first half of 2026, including Rs. 138 billion from sub 1,000cc petrol cars. As pent-up import demand subsides, the phased concession is estimated to cost Rs. 50-60 billion annually, partly offset by higher import volumes as affordable vehicle prices fall.

Part of the revenue loss would be recovered from the opposite end of the vehicle market. Existing import taxation should become progressively heavier for vehicles above 2,000cc, high-powered EVs, luxury SUVs. An Annual Luxury Vehicle Levy might also be considered or a narrow band of high-end vehicles where demand is likely to be inelastic.

National first home fund

Property has traditionally been one of the main ways Sri Lankan families build wealth but increasingly, middle-class Sri Lankans are being priced out of the neighbourhoods in which they grew up. Colombo’s price-to-income ratio is estimated at 55.3 in 2026, according to Numbeo’s Property Price Index; while this measure is distorted due to the urban/rural divide in property prices, it still indicates a lack of affordability. Official and market data show that since 2019, Colombo asking prices have risen approximately 73% for land, 93% for houses and 119% for condominiums while construction costs have also risen by approximately 91%.

Household purchasing power has moved in the opposite direction: Institute of Policy Studies analysis of Department of Census and Statistics data finds that real median household income fell 11.1% between 2019 and early 2025. The result is a widening divide between households that already own appreciating land and property, and younger and middle-class households trying to acquire their first home through salaries and savings. For many middle-class households, the problem is no longer simply the price of a home but also high interest rates, large down-payments and a concentration of new housing supply at the upper end of the market, all making ownership increasingly beyond the reach of even households with stable middle-class incomes. 

The alternative Budget would establish a First Home programme through Bank of Ceylon, People’s Bank, National Savings Bank and the Housing Development Finance Corporation. The treasury would explicitly fund an interest rate subsidy for first time home buyers through the State banks to cover mortgages on concessional rates, subsidising the first 3% or 4% of the mortgage interest rate for say, the first 5 to 7 years. Support would decline as household income rises.

A first-home mortgage could apply to properties valued at up to Rs. 30-35 million and the subsidised mortgage would cover up to 80% of the purchase price, subject to a maximum subsidised loan of Rs. 20 million. Buyers purchasing properties above Rs. 25 million would therefore need to finance the additional amount through their own funds or borrowing at normal commercial rates. Repayment periods could extend up to 25 years. Eligibility would be restricted to the purchase of a first residential property, with an indicative household income ceiling of Rs. 600,000-750,000 per month. Similar policies have been in place in many countries including India, Malaysia and Indonesia. 

A Rent-to-Own Housing Program would allow part of a household’s monthly housing payment to accumulate as equity, for example, on a monthly payment of Rs. 80,000, Rs. 50,000 could cover rent and financing costs while Rs. 30,000 is credited to a Home Equity Account. After five years, the household would have accumulated Rs. 1.8 million towards purchasing the property. After ten years, this would rise to Rs. 3.6 million, before any Government matching contribution, and for lower-middle-income first-home buyers, the State could match part of these accumulated savings. 

The Government’s principal contribution need not be a large cash subsidy. Well-located State land around railway stations and major transport corridors could be leased for medium-density housing, with private developers selected through competitive tenders; keeping land under public ownership would remove a major component of development costs and reduce apartment prices.

Mortgage and rent-to-own programs must also increase housing supply, subsidising demand without expanding supply risks simply pushing up property prices. Subsidised units should therefore be developed alongside new housing and carry temporary resale restrictions to prevent speculation. The objective is to expand affordable middle-class housing and create a realistic path from renting to home ownership.

Middle-class relief within the fiscal anchor

Budget 2027 projects that direct taxes would contribute only 24% to total tax revenue while indirect taxes would account for 76%; a ratio that has consistently hovered between 80:20 and 70:30, always in favour of indirect taxes like VAT and import duties. Indirect taxes are regressive by nature, ie, they impact low income groups disproportionately.

For the middle class, the damage is not captured by poverty statistics but households have experienced a profound deterioration in their standard of living. A family can remain employed and technically middle-income while losing the ability to save, purchase a home, finance a vehicle, educate its children privately, travel, invest in a business or accumulate assets. 

That is the economic space in which aspiration withers. This is where opposition to AKD and the NPP Government will converge, joining farming communities including those that held a protest on the 2nd of November in Anuradhapura or the Government Service Engineers’ Association that held a nationwide strike on the 13 of November. The Main Opposition SJB is uniquely placed to take advantage of a potential middle-class revolt against the Government, given its strong middle-class bases in electorates such as Dehiwala, Kandy, Galle, Matara, Kurunegala, Badulla, Bandarawela and so on.

Any alternative Budget operating within the present debt sustainability framework would have to retain the fiscal anchor: Sri Lanka is committed to returning to a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP from 2027. The alternative Budget would not therefore abandon fiscal consolidation but it would alter the composition of revenue and expenditure within the fiscal anchor.

The objective should be broadly revenue neutral middle-class relief. The alternative Budget would match the 2027 Budget’s Rs.162,500 monthly tax-free threshold, but provide substantially greater relief immediately above the threshold through lower marginal income tax rates. This avoids narrowing the tax base further while reducing the burden on lower and middle-income earners. 

Part of the revenue loss would be recovered through higher marginal rates on very high incomes and stronger collection from high-income taxpayers outside salaried employment. Revenue neutrality should apply to the overall tax package rather than requiring PIT reform to be exactly revenue neutral; corporate taxation, VAT, property and luxury taxation, improved compliance and other revenue measures will also contribute. The 2027 Budget estimates Rs. 210 billion from PAYE/APIT and Rs. 95 billion from other non-corporate income tax, giving total non-corporate income-tax revenue of Rs. 305 billion.

* Note: these are marginal rates: higher rates apply only to income within each specific band

Relief is concentrated on lower and middle-income taxpayers and declines as incomes rise. The 40% and 42% top rates are transitional, with a three-year review allowing thresholds or rates to be adjusted if growth and revenue performance permit.

Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT)

Income tax not collected at source is generally settled through self-assessment, including quarterly instalments and a final payment. Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT) on employment income is deducted directly by employers and remitted to the IRD, making it one of the more reliable methods of collecting personal income tax.

Under the alternative Budget, APIT withholding tables would be adjusted to reflect the new marginal rates; the proposed 40% and 42% rates on the highest bracket of employment incomes would therefore be collected progressively through payroll during the year. APIT is not an additional tax so amounts withheld are credited against the taxpayer’s final income-tax liability, improving collection certainty while reducing the risk of unpaid tax and creating no additional taxes on the tax payer. 

The Rs. 3.7 million annual-income category begins at approximately Rs. 308,000 per month and includes both middle-income professionals receiving tax relief and higher earners facing the proposed 40% and 42% rates. Available APIT data are insufficient to determine whether the higher rates would fully offset the revenue loss, requiring final calibration against detailed IRD data. The 10% withholding tax on interest would remain unchanged for ordinary savers, with a higher rate applying only to very large interest incomes.

The higher withholding remains creditable against final PIT liability and should not automatically be counted as additional permanent revenue; its main purpose is to collect a larger proportion of the eventual tax liability earlier and reduce collection risk. The Rs.10 million threshold would have to apply to aggregate interest income across financial institutions rather than separately at each bank.

The alternative Budget would be an attempt to rebuild the ladder of middle-class asset ownership that has been severely damaged by the economic crisis: income becomes savings; savings become a deposit; a deposit becomes a home; work makes a family car attainable; and rising income once again produces a material improvement in living standards. That is what restoring aspiration must look like, and the national Budget must reflect this.

(The writer is a political commentator, media presenter, and foreign affairs analyst. A former banker, he spent 11 years in the industry in Colombo and Dubai, including nine years in corporate finance, working with some of Sri Lanka’s largest corporates on project finance, trade facilities, and working capital. He holds a Master’s in International Relations from the University of Colombo and a Bachelor’s in Accounting and Finance from the University of Kent (UK). He currently serves as Advisor on Political Economy to the Leader of the Opposition of Sri Lanka, and is a member of the Working Committee of the Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB). title: Anuradhapura: Protecting our ancient water civilisation, archaeological heritage and national land | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 02:52
-     - 18

We are guardians and not owners: the wisdom of King Devanampiya Tissa, the principles articulated by Justice C.G. Weeramantry and the landmark reasoning of Justice A.R.B. Amerasinghe convey a common message. Our ancestors did not build reservoirs, canals, monasteries and sacred monuments merely for their own generation. They created a civilisation to be preserved and passed on

The wisdom of Justices A.R.B. Amerasinghe and C.G. Weeramantry directing decisions affecting the sacred city of Anuradhapura

Anuradhapura is replete with historical marvels; some of the marvels identified by the generations of yesteryear require national and public attention to protect and preserve them for the generations yet unborn.

One of those marvels is the Kalawewa National Park in Kekirawa, a sanctuary for elephants, particularly tuskers, which are rare in the country. In the dry season, the water levels of the reservoirs recede, revealing green grasslands that attract elephants. The Kala Wewa and Balalu Wewa reservoirs, built in the 5th century, are central to the park's ecosystem. The massive Kumbuk trees that line the park are a habitat for numerous birds, both resident and migratory.

Another marvel is the Yoda Ela, an 87 km (54 mi) long single-banking water canal constructed in 459 AD, carrying excess water from the Kala Wewa reservoir in Anuradhapura to the Tissa Wewa reservoir. The Yoda Ela is acclaimed for its low gradient of 6 inches per mile which, even with modern-day survey equipment, would be a difficult feat to achieve with such accuracy.

Then there is the ‘Biso Kotuwa’, an ancient Sri Lankan hydraulic valve pit system used to regulate water pressure and flow in the large reservoirs, preventing embankment damage and ensuring controlled irrigation. Such systems are found in sites like Polonnaruwa, Sigiriya and Anuradhapura, and comprise a vertical valve chamber built inside or beside a reservoir sluice. The pressure-dissipating mechanism reduces destructive water velocity before release and was constructed using precisely cut stone blocks, often without mortar. The system is considered to be one of the most advanced ancient hydraulic inventions.

Two respected judges, Justice Amerasinghe and Justice Weeramantry, in judgments delivered independently in two different cases, emphasised that Anuradhapura is not simply an archaeological city or a destination for tourism; it represents one of the world's remarkable ancient hydraulic civilisations, where water management, agriculture, religious heritage, engineering and environmental conservation were developed as one integrated system.

Anuradhapura's ancient reservoirs, canals, waterways, catchment areas, forests, elephants, Buddhist monuments and archaeological remains form an interconnected national heritage.

In a landmark judgment issued in the Eppawela Phosphate case of 2000 (Bulankulama and others vs Freeport-McMoRan and others), Justice Amerasinghe, with two other learned Justices of the Supreme Court in agreement, stated without ambiguity that any development that affects this heritage must be considered not merely as an exercise in planning, economics or tourism, but as a matter of national responsibility, environmental protection and the rule of law.

Government is the temporary custodian and cannot distribute State land

In this landmark judgment, Justice Amerasinghe examined the proposed phosphate mining project in the Anuradhapura District.

The Court considered the potential consequences for the ancient irrigation systems of Rajarata, the water and soil conservation ecosystems, underground aquifers and agricultural lands, the archaeological and cultural heritage and the livelihoods of local communities.

One particularly important observation concerned the inadequacy of existing legal protection for the cultural-heritage landscape.

Justice Amerasinghe drew attention to the fact that there was no adequate provision for protecting a cultural-heritage landscape such as the Yoda Wewa, as distinct from an individual archaeological monument.

Justice Amerasinghe went on to say that protecting an individual dagoba or monument is not necessarily sufficient if the surrounding ancient irrigation system, landscape, waterways and archaeological setting are damaged.

The judgment also emphasised the precautionary approach towards sustainable development and the principle that environmental damage must be borne by those responsible for causing it. The judgment deemed that if no plans are publicly available, there is no way to assess the damage that could possibly be caused by the project; in these circumstances, a project is not to be proceeded with.

Justice Amerasinghe's judgment says that Sri Lanka's law cannot be circumvented by secret agreements or by some type of understanding arrived at by two parties to the contract.

The judgment went on to say that the authority that will determine whether a project is suitable for the country in respect of its heritage, civilisation, environment, etc., is the authority that has been delegated such powers by the country's sovereign law.

Sri Lanka's ancient water wisdom recognised internationally

In 1997, Justice C.G. Weeramantry, a former Vice-President of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), made a similar observation in a case that came up before him at the ICJ. Sri Lanka's ancient water wisdom was internationally recognised.

In the Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project case (Hungary vs. Slovakia), which came up before the ICJ in 1997, Justice Weeramantry referred extensively to Sri Lanka's ancient irrigation civilisation. He explained how Sri Lanka's ancient rulers developed a sophisticated system of reservoirs and canals while recognising the need to conserve nature.

The eminent judge referred to the ancient principle that not even a small quantity of rainwater should flow to the sea without benefiting the people.

Justice Weeramantry also referred to the sermon of Arahat Mahinda to King Devanampiya Tissa, explaining that animals and birds have an equal right to live and move within the land.

Justice Weeramantry's central message was that development and environmental conservation must go together. He recognised that sustainable development was not a newly invented international concept: Sri Lanka had practiced these principles for centuries.

The connection between these two eminent judges

An important point is that Justice Amerasinghe's Eppawela judgment referred to Justice Weeramantry's international jurisprudence.

Their contributions provide a powerful legal and historical foundation for the principle that development and environmental conservation must go hand in hand.

Public Trust doctrine

Justice Amerasinghe and Justice Weeramantry both outline the doctrine of ‘Public Trust’, nationally and internationally.

This doctrine carries an intergenerational responsibility: the responsibility to protect natural resources.

The two eminent judges speak of sustainable development, the need to protect the Yoda Wewa cultural landscape, the ancient irrigation wisdom, the precautionary approach to environmental damage, harmony between development and nature, including the fauna, the flora and the majestic elephants that roam the land, and the shared responsibility to protect them all for future generations.

Together, the wisdom of the honourable judges provides an important framework for examining development projects in Anuradhapura and elsewhere.

Why the present Anuradhapura development proposals require careful examination

The ancient city cannot be separated from its water civilisation. A proper assessment must consider whether proposed development could affect the archaeological remains and ancient monuments; ancient tanks, canals and irrigation channels; water catchment areas and groundwater; the historical landscape surrounding sacred monuments; the ecological balance and traditional agricultural environment; and the integrity and religious character of the sacred city.

The protection of heritage should not be confined to individual monuments while the wider historic landscape and the habitat of elephants and other animals and birds are altered.

Applicable legal protection

The following laws should be examined together: the Antiquities Ordinance No. 9 of 1940 (protection of antiquities, ancient monuments and archaeological reserves); the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980 (environmental approvals and assessment, where applicable); the State Lands Ordinance No. 8 of 1947 (legal administration of State land); and the Mahaweli Authority of Sri Lanka Act No. 23 of 1979 (where applicable, to designated areas and lands).

Also important are Article 27(14) of the Constitution (State responsibility to protect, preserve and improve the environment) and Article 28(f) (the duty of every person to protect nature and conserve its riches). The Eppawela judgment is particularly important when applying these laws to development proposals affecting interconnected archaeological and environmental resources.

The central question for the Government

Can a Government undertake tourism and infrastructure development in Anuradhapura without first establishing, through proper archaeological, hydrological and environmental studies, that the ancient water systems, archaeological landscape and sacred character will be protected?

The answers must be provided by the legal principles already established by our courts.

Conclusion

We are guardians and not owners: the wisdom of King Devanampiya Tissa, the principles articulated by Justice C.G. Weeramantry and the landmark reasoning of Justice A.R.B. Amerasinghe convey a common message.

Our ancestors did not build reservoirs, canals, monasteries and sacred monuments merely for their own generation. They created a civilisation to be preserved and passed on.

Anuradhapura is not simply land available for development. It is a national inheritance held in trust for generations yet unborn.

It is the Government's duty to preserve its archaeological integrity, ancient water civilisation, sacred character and historical landscape. Development must serve this heritage, not destroy or diminish it.

(The author is a Senior Attorney-at-Law who has worked with Justice A.R.B. Amerasinghe.)

title: Growth deadlock: Diagnosing Sri Lanka’s detour from knowledge economy and charting the way forward - Part I | Daily FT
summary:
