-     - 18

Presidential Address delivered at the Annual International Conference 2026 of the Sri Lanka Economic Association (SLEA), held on 21 November, 2026

The theme of the Annual International Conference 2026 of the Sri Lanka Economic Association (SLEA) is not just relevant but absolutely vital for our nation's survival and future prosperity: "Paving the Way for Sri Lanka's Knowledge Economy". The country has been caught in the lower-middle-income trap for the last three decades. What went wrong for Sri Lanka? My answer can be encapsulated in two terms - "low productivity" and "closed economy".

Diminishing returns on investment

The Sri Lankan economy's low productivity is due to the diminishing returns on capital. In 1960, we required only three units of capital to produce one additional unit of output or GDP. Today we have to invest six units to yield the same output increase of one unit. This implies diminishing marginal returns on investment.

Land, labour and capital have been the major drivers of Sri Lanka's GDP growth so far. We have invested heavily in factories, machinery and other physical capital only to gain diminishing marginal returns. As a result, the economy remains at a low equilibrium level. The only way to expand the country's production possibility frontier is to introduce knowledge inputs into our growth model.

Sri Lanka getting isolated from the global economy

Low productivity, coupled with inward-looking economic strategies, has eroded export competitiveness, and Sri Lanka has now become a more closed economy. Its exports-to-GDP ratio came down from 27% in 1960 to just 14% in 2025. This means we are getting more and more isolated from the rest of the world.

The resulting low GDP growth not only prevents improvement in people's quality of life but also disturbs macroeconomic stability, which is the very foundation of economic prosperity.

Knowledge-driven growth is the obvious choice

As we look back at the economic shocks of the recent past, it has become abundantly clear that Sri Lanka can no longer rely solely on traditional, resource-dependent economic models. The global economic landscape is changing rapidly. Wealth is no longer dictated just by physical capital or raw labour, but by the generation, dissemination and application of knowledge. For Sri Lanka to unlock shock-resilient and sustainable long-term growth, a structural transition towards a knowledge-driven economy is the obvious choice.

Theoretical foundation

Knowledge-driven growth is rooted in Endogenous Growth Theory, developed by Paul Romer in 1990. It treats human capital, innovation and technological progress as internal drivers of economic growth, overcoming the diminishing returns of physical capital through non-rival public goods. Unlike physical machines or land, knowledge can be used simultaneously by multiple people and firms without wearing out or depleting. This creates increasing marginal returns rather than diminishing returns to scale.

The older neoclassical models articulated by Robert Solow in 1956 asserted that technology fell 'from the sky' as an exogenous shock. In contrast, new growth models internalise research and development (R&D), education and spillovers as deliberate economic choices. Accordingly, long-run growth mainly depends on internally generated technological change by means of the key drivers - human capital, knowledge and R&D.

5th Industrial Revolution

The present era of the 5th Industrial Revolution (5IR or Industry 5.0) is a value-driven system that prioritises the synergy between human intelligence and advanced technology. While the 4th Industrial Revolution (4IR) focused on automation and efficiency, the 5IR shifts the focus back to human-centricity, sustainability and resilience. In this context, a knowledge economy that creates, disseminates and uses knowledge is essential to accelerate Sri Lanka's export-led growth and to escape the middle-income trap.

Pillars of knowledge economy

To guide the deliberations in the technical sessions of this Conference, we focus on four foundational pillars that must be strengthened to secure this transition:

Sri Lanka's dismal economic growth

Let us now look at the growth performance of Sri Lanka. Since the economic liberalisation policies adopted in late 1977, the annual average growth rate has hovered around 4%. Overall, GDP growth shows a declining trend during the period from 1977 to date.

The average growth fluctuated significantly during this period, and it crossed the 8% mark only on two occasions. The first was in 1978, reflecting the pent-up demand that emerged immediately after liberalisation. The second outlier came in the three years following the cessation of the war in 2009 and was mainly caused by reconstruction activities. These growth spikes could not last long as they were not based on any structural transformation of the economy.

The growth rate was in the negative region during 2019-2023 (except in 2021) amidst the COVID-19 pandemic and the economic crisis. The economic reforms adopted since 2022 helped the economy recover, as reflected in the moderate growth rate of 5% in 2024 and 2025. This recovery appears to be short-lived. For this year, the growth rate is expected to decline to 3.2%, according to official forecasts.

Fast-growing East Asian economies

Sri Lanka's growth performance is dismal in comparison with the fast-growing East Asian countries. Between 1960 and 2025, the economic landscape of these countries underwent a dramatic transformation, in contrast to Sri Lanka. While Japan and the Four Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong) achieved extraordinary leaps in per capita wealth, Sri Lanka followed a volatile, low-growth trajectory.

At the time of its independence, Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) had a higher per capita income than South Korea and was widely seen as a prospective economic model. However, differing choices in industrialisation strategy, political stability and total factor productivity led to a profound developmental divergence over the next six decades.

Since the early 1960s, Japan and the Four Asian Tigers have transformed from war-torn, developing agrarian societies into high-income global powerhouses. Their per capita GDP skyrocketed from a range of $ 150 to $ 520 in 1960 to high-income levels ranging from $ 36,000 to nearly $ 100,000 today.

East Asian development model

Japan pioneered the "East Asian Developmental Model", using State-directed capitalism, aggressive export-oriented manufacturing and massive investment in technology to resurrect its economy.

South Korea shifted aggressively from an agrarian economy to a global electronics and heavy-industry manufacturing hub, mainly by using technology and innovation. Its per capita GDP of $ 155 in 1960, which was marginally above Sri Lanka's per capita GDP of $ 146, grew exponentially to 

$ 36,227 by 2025. Today, Sri Lanka's per capita GDP is only $ 5,000.

Singapore and Hong Kong capitalised on their strategic maritime locations to transition into world-class trade, logistics and financial centres. By 2025, Singapore surged to lead Asia with a per capita GDP close to $ 100,000, while Hong Kong reached $ 56,983.

Growth hindrances

Sri Lanka, which had a comparable or higher economic baseline than some of its East Asian peers in the 1950s and early 1960s, experienced slower, volatile growth marred by a multitude of negative factors, including dogmatic political ideologies, prolonged ethnic conflict, civil unrest, inconsistent economic policies, structural bottlenecks, politically affiliated trade union protests, labour indiscipline and macroeconomic imbalances. Sri Lanka's per capita GDP crawled from $ 146 in 1960 to a mere $ 5,002 in 2025.

Middle-income trap

Sri Lanka transitioned from a low-income country to a lower-middle-income country in 1997 and has remained in this category, except on two brief occasions. It first graduated to upper-middle-income status in 2019, but the achievement was short-lived as it was placed back in the lower-middle-income category the following year against the backdrop of the economic crisis.

More recently, Sri Lanka was promoted to the upper-middle-income category for the second time in July 2026. With a per capita Gross National Income (GNI) of $ 4,670 in 2025, the country cleared the upper-middle-income threshold of $ 4,636 by a narrow margin of $ 34 per person. Overall, the country has been trapped in the middle-income category, mostly as a lower-middle-income country, for three decades.

(The author is the President of the Sri Lanka Economic Association and Emeritus Professor in Economics at the Open University of Sri Lanka)

Having entered the final undefeated across seven matches of the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy, Sri Lanka are within a cusp of lifting a trophy for women’s cricket without their most experienced and iconic player Chamari Athapaththu when they take on Ireland in the final at Karwan SC cricket ground, Ajman today.

Sri Lanka has not won so many finals in women’s cricket but in the few they have, Athapaththu has been at the helm. She had to miss out on the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy due to her commitment with Hobart Hurricanes in the Women’s Big Bash League.

For Sri Lanka women’s next generation of cricketers led by Harshitha Samarawickrama a win against Ireland will give the team the confidence that they can absorb pressure and win a tournament final sans Athapaththu who has been the beacon of the team for quite a number of years and on whose success the career of these young women are built.

Harshitha has turned out to be a proven leader as the results of the matches played so far in the tournament imply and the player most likely to succeed once Athapaththu decides to call it a day.

Sri Lanka’s success in the tournament has overshadowed Harshitha’s poor form with the bat. In the six innings she has played so far she has passed 20 only twice. A big score is overdue from her and what better occasion than a final to do it? It is imperative that Harshitha gets some runs behind her because her lack of contribution has made the Sri Lankan middle order rather vulnerable.

Harshitha’s paucity of runs has more or less been compensated by opener Vishmi Gunaratne. The elegant right-hander is going through a purple patch in her career. With scores of 53*, 49, 51, 63*, 39*, 29* and 30 she is the leading run-getter in the tournament with 314 runs at an average of 104.66. Hasini Perera and Imesha Dulani are the only other players to score a half-century in the tournament for Sri Lanka.  

Sri Lanka’s strength lies in their bowling where seamer Sathya Sandeepani and versatile spinner Kavisha Dilhari have been outstanding, each having taken 13 wickets at less than five runs an over. Left-arm spinners Nimasha Meepage, a late replacement for injured Chamudi Praboda and Sugandika Kumari have also been amongst the wickets taking 8 wickets apiece. This quartet has formed the backbone of the Lankan bowling attack.

One area where Sri Lanka needs to improve if they are to give Ireland a good run is their fielding. Their catching against Bangladesh in their final Super Over match was appalling, spilling five which is inexcusable at this level of cricket.

Ireland on the other hand are quite happy the way they have progressed to the final. Their Captain Gaby Lewis believes confidence is rising for her side as they head for the final. Ireland’s victory over the Netherlands in their final Super Six game qualified them for a place in the final. It was their third straight win of the Super Six phase and Lewis thinks her team is getting better with every appearance in the tournament.      

While Sri Lanka have yet to taste defeat during the tournament, Ireland had to earn their place in the title decider via a somewhat different route given they failed to take any points across to the Super Six phase from the initial group stage.

Ireland split four matches during that first group stage - with victories against the UAE and Papua New Guinea offset by losses to Sri Lanka in the tournament opener and Scotland - leaving them with a trio of must-win contests across the Super Sixes that culminated in a winner-take-all clash with the Netherlands.

“I think we knew coming in that we could beat the three teams ahead (in the Super Six phase),” said Lewis. “I think we had a lot of confidence with parts of our performance in the group stages, but we just didn't have that whole team performance. We just took it game by game and I think we're on a bit of a streak now. So here's to one more (win).”

While Lewis looms as Ireland's key player heading into the final against Sri Lanka, with the second highest aggregate 264 runs (avg. 37.71), it's Cara Murray who could well prove the wildcard in the eagerly-awaited contest. The right-arm leg-spinner has 15 scalps (econ rate 5.52) for her side across the tournament to be the second leading wicket-taker in the tournament.

The first meeting between the two teams in the group stage saw Sri Lanka overwhelm Ireland by 10 wickets at the same venue chasing down 106 in 13 overs with unbeaten half-centuries from Hasini Perera and Vishmi Gunaratne. But since then Ireland has grown in confidence as the tournament progressed and Sri Lanka can expect much stiffer competition in the final.

summary:

Gaurav Bahirvani with former Sri Lanka captain Arjuna Ranatunga at the SSC during Test Twenty

They called him the Jerry Maguire of India. Gaurav Bahirvani spent years in Britain working in brand valuation before getting his break in sport handling MS Dhoni’s commercial interests. But the player who got him thinking about launching his own cricket competition was his 13-year-old son, Waris.

Watching boys of his son’s age train in India, Bahirvani was struck by how much of their cricket revolved around the white ball. “These kids, when they go to the academies, they’re playing with a white ball,” he said. “They have been taught to come out and hit.”

In December 2024, on an Emirates flight back to India, he typed ‘Test Twenty’ into his phone and began working through the rules of Test cricket and T20. The result was four innings of up to 20 overs in a day. Each side bats once in whites against the red ball and again in coloured kit against the white ball under lights. The first-innings scores carry forward.

Bahirvani initially planned separate competitions for boys and girls. Sony, he said, could accommodate about eight hours for one match, including coverage either side of play. Two fixtures would have taken twice as long. His solution was to give each team a boys’ XI and a girls’ XI, with both contributing to the same result. The captain who wins the toss chooses whether to bat or bowl and which XI plays first. The other inherits the lead or deficit. “It’s absolute parity,” Bahirvani said.

Sir Clive Lloyd asked how a match could end in a draw. Bahirvani says he wrote the rule at three in the morning. The side batting fourth can save the match by seeing out its overs with no more than four wickets down. Once the fifth falls, the draw is gone.

Sri Lanka stepped in to host after conflict in the region made some parents uneasy about sending their children to Abu Dhabi, Bahirvani said. He wants the tournament to stay in Sri Lanka for at least three years.

The inaugural season drew more than 15,000 applications from 27 countries, he said. The shortlist was cut to 1,000, with 300 going into the draft. Four continental squads were picked, each with 20 boys and 20 girls.

The other 700 go into a development pool, with coaching camps and master classes planned. Bahirvani also wants tournaments across seven regions, with Sri Lanka as the South Asian hub. Performances there could earn youngsters a place in the next draft.

“Every league is a buyer,” he said. “Nobody owns the factory.”

The same rules apply at home. Waris did not play in the first season and will have to come through the trials if he wants a place.

title: Heritance Tea Factory celebrates 30 years of living tea heritage in Sri Lanka’s highlands | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 02:37
-     - 6

Heritance Tea Factory marks its 30th anniversary on 24 November 2026, celebrating three decades since a former 19th century tea factory in the highlands of Kandapola was given a remarkable second life. 

Since opening as The Tea Factory in 1996, the property has grown into one of Sri Lanka’s most distinctive heritage hotels, preserving the industrial story of Ceylon tea while creating an experience deeply connected to the landscape and communities that surround it.

The building’s story, however, stretches back much further. Hethersett Estate traces its origins to 1879, when English planter William Flowerdew acquired land in Sri Lanka’s central highlands and named the estate after his hometown in England. Tea gradually became central to the estate, with an early factory established in the late 19th century and the present structure taking shape following reconstruction in the 1930s. For decades, it processed tea grown across the surrounding hills before production ceased in 1973.

Nearly two decades later, Aitken Spence recognised the potential of the abandoned building. Rather than replace it, the company chose to preserve its industrial character and adapt the original structure and features for an entirely new purpose. In 1996, the building reopened as The Tea Factory, more than 2,000 metres above sea level, setting an early benchmark for adaptive reuse within Sri Lankan hospitality.

Today, up to 70% of the hotel’s team comes from surrounding communities, bringing local knowledge and a lived connection to tea country into everyday guest interactions. This approach was recognised in 2026, when Heritance Tea Factory received the award for Championing Cultural Diversity at the ICRT Indian Subcontinent Responsible Tourism Awards. That sense of place is carried through the people who shape the guest experience, and is woven through the fabric of the hotel itself.

The original structure remains visible throughout the hotel today. The former withering lofts, once used to dry freshly harvested tea leaves, became guest rooms, while the tall windows continue to bring light into the building and frame sweeping views across tea country. Original steelwork, timber floors, machinery and industrial details remain woven into the interiors. The former sifting room became the Kenmare Restaurant, while spaces once associated with weighing and packing tea continue their story through the Hethersett Bar.

Over time, new experiences have been introduced without losing sight of that heritage. TCK 6685, the restored railway carriage now turned fine dining restaurant, recalls the relationship between Sri Lanka’s railways and the movement of tea from the highlands. The Mini Tea Factory takes guests through the journey from leaf to cup, while tea plucking, tasting, high tea and walks through the surrounding estate and the world-famous Pekoe Trail make tea culture something to participate in rather than simply observe.

In 2009, the property entered its next chapter as Heritance Tea Factory, strengthening its focus on experiences rooted in place, heritage and responsible hospitality.

Environmental responsibility has similarly become part of the property’s evolution. Initiatives including biomass energy, solar thermal systems, heat recovery, wastewater reuse, rainwater harvesting and organic cultivation reflect a philosophy of preserving not only a building, but the wider environment in which it exists.

Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC Chairperson Stasshani Jayawardena said:  “Heritance Tea Factory represents what can happen when heritage is preserved with purpose. Few places in the world offer an experience quite like Heritance Tea Factory, where the character of an original tea factory has been preserved and reimagined as a heritage hotel. Today, its value lies not only in what has been preserved physically, but in the connections it continues to create between guests, communities and Sri Lanka’s tea heritage.”

Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC Managing Director Susith Jayawickrama said:  “From the outset, The Tea Factory was an unconventional idea. Its success over three decades demonstrates the enduring value of respecting the character of a place. As we celebrate 30 years, we recognise the teams, communities, guests and partners who have carried this story forward while continuing to evolve the experience for a new generation of travellers.”

That commitment has earned the property recognition across architecture, conservation, heritage and responsible tourism, including a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Merit Award, a PATA Grand Award for Heritage and Culture, and recognition as Sri Lanka’s Leading Heritage Hotel at the World Travel Awards.

Thirty years after welcoming its first guests, Heritance Tea Factory remains a place where the building’s original purpose has never disappeared. It can still be seen in its machinery, tasted in its tea, heard in the stories of its people and experienced across the landscape beyond its windows.
